claim: The survival prognosis of HPV-positive and HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is largely different.
source: The survival prognosis of human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive and HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is largely different, and little is known about the anti-tumor mechanism of tumor-infiltrated exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tex) in HNSCC.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: A proliferative exhausted CD8+ T cell cluster (P-Tex) which was beneficial to survival outcomes of patients with HPV-positive HNSCC was identified.
source: A proliferative exhausted CD8+ T cell cluster (P-Tex) which was beneficial to survival outcomes of patients with HPV-positive HNSCC was identified.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from scRNA-seq and survival analysis.

claim: P-Tex cells expressed CDK4 genes as high as cancer cells.
source: Interestingly, P-Tex cells expressed CDK4 genes as high as cancer cells, which could be simultaneously inhibited by CDK4 inhibitors and might be a potential reason for the ineffectiveness of CDK4 inhibitors in treating HPV-positive HNSCC.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing CDK4 expression levels and in vitro experiments with CDK4 inhibitors.

claim: P-Tex cells could be simultaneously inhibited by CDK4 inhibitors.
source: Interestingly, P-Tex cells expressed CDK4 genes as high as cancer cells, which could be simultaneously inhibited by CDK4 inhibitors and might be a potential reason for the ineffectiveness of CDK4 inhibitors in treating HPV-positive HNSCC.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experiments showing that abemaciclib inhibited the cell viability of both cancer cells and P-Tex cells.

claim: The inhibition of P-Tex cells by CDK4 inhibitors might be a potential reason for the ineffectiveness of CDK4 inhibitors in treating HPV-positive HNSCC.
source: Interestingly, P-Tex cells expressed CDK4 genes as high as cancer cells, which could be simultaneously inhibited by CDK4 inhibitors and might be a potential reason for the ineffectiveness of CDK4 inhibitors in treating HPV-positive HNSCC.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the inference from experimental data and clinical observations.

claim: P-Tex cells could aggregate in the antigen-presenting cell niches.
source: P-Tex cells could aggregate in the antigen-presenting cell niches and activate certain signaling pathways.
evidence: This is supported by spatial transcriptomics and multiplex immunofluorescence data showing co-localization of P-Tex cells with APCs.

claim: P-Tex cells activate certain signaling pathways in antigen-presenting cell niches.
source: P-Tex cells could aggregate in the antigen-presenting cell niches and activate certain signaling pathways.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis showing enrichment of T cell activation and proliferation signaling pathways in APC areas.

claim: P-Tex cells provide modest but persistent anti-tumor effects in HPV-positive HNSCC.
source: Together, our findings suggest a promising role for P-Tex cells in the prognosis of patients with HPV-positive HNSCC by providing modest but persistent anti-tumor effects.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the combination of survival data, in vitro experiments showing prolonged cell survival, and functional characterization.

claim: The incidence of HNSCC has continued to rise with an annual increase of 1.08 million new cases estimated by 2030.
source: The incidence of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) has continued to rise and an annual increase of 1.08 million new cases is estimated by 2030, which is greatly attributed to the increasing rates of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection (Bray et al., 2018; Ferlay et al., 2019; Näsman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: The increasing incidence of HNSCC is greatly attributed to the increasing rates of HPV infection.
source: The incidence of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) has continued to rise and an annual increase of 1.08 million new cases is estimated by 2030, which is greatly attributed to the increasing rates of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection (Bray et al., 2018; Ferlay et al., 2019; Näsman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: HPV-positive HNSCC and HPV-negative HNSCC displayed markedly different characteristics from pathogenesis to treatment outcomes.
source: HPV-positive HNSCC and HPV-negative HNSCC displayed markedly different characteristics from pathogenesis to treatment outcomes and are visualized as two distinct clinical entities (Ang et al., 2010; Wansom et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: HPV-positive HNSCC and HPV-negative HNSCC are visualized as two distinct clinical entities.
source: HPV-positive HNSCC and HPV-negative HNSCC displayed markedly different characteristics from pathogenesis to treatment outcomes and are visualized as two distinct clinical entities (Ang et al., 2010; Wansom et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: T cell exhaustion within the tumor microenvironment results from persistent antigen stimulation from chronic virus infection or tumors.
source: T cell exhaustion within the tumor microenvironment (TME) is a newly discovered phenomenon resulting from persistent antigen stimulation from chronic virus infection or tumors, in which tumor-infiltrated CD8+ T cells experience gradual alterations in their functional capacity while highly expressing multiple inhibitory receptors, including PD1, TIM3, LAG3, CTLA4, and TIGIT (Wherry and Kurachi, 2015; Blank et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on T cell exhaustion.

claim: Tumor-infiltrated CD8+ T cells in exhaustion experience gradual alterations in their functional capacity while highly expressing multiple inhibitory receptors, including PD1, TIM3, LAG3, CTLA4, and TIGIT.
source: T cell exhaustion within the tumor microenvironment (TME) is a newly discovered phenomenon resulting from persistent antigen stimulation from chronic virus infection or tumors, in which tumor-infiltrated CD8+ T cells experience gradual alterations in their functional capacity while highly expressing multiple inhibitory receptors, including PD1, TIM3, LAG3, CTLA4, and TIGIT (Wherry and Kurachi, 2015; Blank et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on T cell exhaustion.

claim: Heterogeneity is a hallmark of T cell exhaustion.
source: Recent studies have revealed that heterogeneity is a hallmark of T cell exhaustion, and several distinct subsets of exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tex) have been identified, each with unique gene signatures, functional characteristics, and epigenetic modifications (Miller et al., 2019; Beltra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on T cell exhaustion.

claim: Several distinct subsets of exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tex) have been identified, each with unique gene signatures, functional characteristics, and epigenetic modifications.
source: Recent studies have revealed that heterogeneity is a hallmark of T cell exhaustion, and several distinct subsets of exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tex) have been identified, each with unique gene signatures, functional characteristics, and epigenetic modifications (Miller et al., 2019; Beltra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on T cell exhaustion.

claim: Specific transitions among Tex subsets have been illustrated under certain circumstances and might be associated with retained effector function and enforced tumor control.
source: Meanwhile, specific transitions among those subsets have also been illustrated under certain circumstances and might be associated with retained effector function and enforced tumor control (Im et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on T cell subset transitions.

claim: HPV-positive HNSCC displays a T cell-inflamed phenotype distinct from its HPV-negative counterparts.
source: Recently, there has been increasing evidence showing that HPV-positive HNSCC displays a T cell-inflamed phenotype distinct from its HPV-negative counterparts, indicating that HPV infection is associated with increased T cell infiltration and effector cell activation (Gameiro et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on HPV-positive HNSCC immune phenotypes.

claim: HPV infection is associated with increased T cell infiltration and effector cell activation.
source: Recently, there has been increasing evidence showing that HPV-positive HNSCC displays a T cell-inflamed phenotype distinct from its HPV-negative counterparts, indicating that HPV infection is associated with increased T cell infiltration and effector cell activation (Gameiro et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on HPV-positive HNSCC immune phenotypes.

claim: HPV infection has been proven to be associated with T cell exhaustion.
source: Meanwhile, HPV infection has also been proven to be associated with T cell exhaustion, in which HPV-positive HNSCC expressed higher levels of multiple T cell exhaustion markers such as PD1, TIM3, LAG3, and TIGIT compared to HPV-negative HNSCC, suggesting of stronger antigen-specific T cell immunity in HPV-positive HNSCC (Gameiro et al., 2018; Kansy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on T cell exhaustion in HPV-positive HNSCC.

claim: HPV-positive HNSCC expressed higher levels of multiple T cell exhaustion markers such as PD1, TIM3, LAG3, and TIGIT compared to HPV-negative HNSCC.

claim: CDK4 inhibitors are introduced as novel drugs by targeting and disrupting the CDK4-related cell cycle progression of cancer cells.
source: Cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) inhibitors are introduced as novel drugs by targeting and disrupting the CDK4-related cell cycle progression of cancer cells in recent years (Goel et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on CDK4 inhibitors.

claim: Promising treatment outcomes of CDK4 inhibitors were only observed in HPV-negative HNSCC rather than HPV-positive HNSCC.
source: However, promising treatment outcomes of CDK4 inhibitors were only observed in HPV-negative HNSCC rather than HPV-positive HNSCC (Adkins et al., 2019; Oppelt et al., 2021; van Caloen and Machiels, 2019) due to the mutation differences of cell cycle-related genes in cancer cells, and less attention has been paid to the effects of CDK4 inhibitors on infiltrating T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies on CDK4 inhibitors in HNSCC.

claim: The differential effectiveness of CDK4 inhibitors in HPV-negative versus HPV-positive HNSCC is due to the mutation differences of cell cycle-related genes in cancer cells.

source: A total of 49,813 CD3+ T cells in 14 paired HNSCC tumor and normal adjacent samples were obtained after quality control.

source: And 11 T cell clusters with distinct gene signatures were defined (Figure 1b, Supplementary file 2), including four CD8+ T cell clusters (C1, C4, C7, and C9), five CD4+ T cell clusters (C2: naïve CD4+ T cells, C3: regulatory T cells [Treg], C5: T helper cells, C8: CD4-Tex, and C10: T follicular helper cells), one γδ T cell cluster (C6), and one double negative T cell cluster (C0: DN, CD4-CD8-), with marker genes (Brummelman et al., 2018) shown in Supplementary file 3.

evidence: This is a characterization based on gene expression data and functional scores, with citation support.

claim: C4 showed high expression of checkpoint marker genes, including PDCD1, HAVCR2, LAG3, and TNFRSF9, with both high cytotoxicity and exhaustion scores, which was consistent with the cell identity of terminally differentiated exhausted CD8+ T cells (T-Tex).
source: C4 showed high expression of checkpoint marker genes, including PDCD1, HAVCR2, LAG3, and TNFRSF9, with both high cytotoxicity and exhaustion scores, which was consistent with the cell identity of terminally differentiated exhausted CD8+ T cells (T-Tex) (Wherry and Kurachi, 2015).

claim: C7 and C9 displayed high expression levels of cell cycle-related genes, including CCNA2, UBE2C, and CDK4, as well as stem-like genes MKI67 and ASPM.

evidence: This is a characterization based on gene expression data.

claim: CDK4 was mainly expressed in P-Tex2.
source: More specifically, CDK4 (a canonical cell cycle-related marker gene) was mainly expressed in P-Tex2, whereas MKI67 (the most canonical marker gene for proliferation) was mainly expressed in P-Tex1 (Figure 1e–f), indicating that these two cell clusters might fulfill their proliferative capacity through different mechanisms.
evidence: This is a direct observation from gene expression data shown in figures.

claim: MKI67 was mainly expressed in P-Tex1.

claim: T cell activation, lymphocyte differentiation, and viral gene expression were enriched in all three Tex cell clusters.
source: Specifically, gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis showed that T cell activation, lymphocyte differentiation, and viral gene expression were enriched in all three Tex cell clusters, whereas the regulation of the cell cycle, apoptosis, and certain immune responses were enriched in P-Texs, showing divergent functional specialization (Figure 2a).

claim: Two P-Tex clusters were more enriched in the cell cycle signal pathway than the T-Tex and Teff clusters.

evidence: This is based on GSEA results shown in Figure 2c.

claim: P-Tex1 was mainly in G2/M phase.
source: P-Tex1 was mainly in G2/M phase, indicating cells were under a proliferative burst, which was consistent with the high expression of proliferation marker gene MKI67 (Bertoli et al., 2013), whereas P-Tex2 was mainly in S phase, an essential phase for DNA replication before undergoing mitosis, which was consistent with the high expression of CDK4 (initiating the G1 to S phase transition) (Figure 2e–f; Bertoli et al., 2013; Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2020; Rubin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cell cycle phase analysis shown in Figure 2e-f, with citation support.

claim: P-Tex2 was mainly in S phase.

claim: P-Tex1 and P-Tex2 might represent proliferation cells in two distinct cell cycle phases.
source: Taken together, P-Tex1 and P-Tex2 might represent proliferation cells in two distinct cell cycle phases.

claim: HPV-positive HNSCC patients in TCGA cohort with higher P-Tex score had better survival outcomes (5-year OS: 55.8% vs. 22.6%, p=0.02).

evidence: This is based on TCR clonality analysis shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Hyperexpanded TCR clonotypes were more enriched in tumors than adjacent normal tissues.
source: Our results showed that hyperexpanded TCR clonotypes were more enriched in tumors than adjacent normal tissues (Figure 3c–d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is based on TCR clonality analysis shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: The proportions of hyperexpanded TCR clonotypes of Teff, P-Tex1, and T-Tex showed no significant difference between HPV-positive samples and HPV-negative samples.
source: However, the proportions of hyperexpanded TCR clonotypes of Teff, P-Tex1, and T-Tex showed no significant difference between HPV-positive samples and HPV-negative samples (Figure 3e–f, Figure 3—figure supplement 1e–f).
evidence: This is based on TCR clonality analysis shown in Figure 3e-f.

claim: A higher diversity of TCRs was observed in adjacent normal tissues and HPV-negative samples.
source: Correspondingly, a higher diversity of TCRs was observed in adjacent normal tissues and HPV-negative samples (Figure 3g), indicating the absence of a strong antigen-specific immune response, which further confirmed the crucial roles of virus and tumor play in local T cell proliferation and activation (Hwang et al., 2020; Poropatich et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on TCR diversity analysis shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Higher TCR diversity in adjacent normal tissues and HPV-negative samples indicates the absence of a strong antigen-specific immune response.
source: Correspondingly, a higher diversity of TCRs was observed in adjacent normal tissues and HPV-negative samples (Figure 3g), indicating the absence of a strong antigen-specific immune response, which further confirmed the crucial roles of virus and tumor play in local T cell proliferation and activation (Hwang et al., 2020; Poropatich et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on TCR diversity analysis with citation support.

claim: Most of the shared TCRs were observed among the T-Tex, P-Tex, and Teff clusters.
source: We further examined the TCR clonotype occupation among each cluster and revealed that most of the shared TCRs were observed among the T-Tex, P-Tex, and Teff clusters (Figure 3h–i, Supplementary files 6-7).
evidence: This is based on TCR sharing analysis shown in Figure 3h-i.

claim: The Teff cluster had higher proportion of TCRs shared with the γδ T (overlap coefficient, oc = 0.49), Tex (oc = 0.43), P-Tex2 (oc = 0.35), and P-Tex1 (oc = 0.33) clusters, respectively.
source: The Teff cluster had higher proportion of TCRs shared with the γδ T (overlap coefficient, oc = 0.49), Tex (oc = 0.43), P-Tex2 (oc = 0.35), and P-Tex1 (oc = 0.33) clusters, respectively, indicating they had common ancestry of origin.
evidence: This is based on TCR overlap analysis.

claim: TCR sharing between Teff and other clusters indicates they had common ancestry of origin.
source: The Teff cluster had higher proportion of TCRs shared with the γδ T (overlap coefficient, oc = 0.49), Tex (oc = 0.43), P-Tex2 (oc = 0.35), and P-Tex1 (oc = 0.33) clusters, respectively, indicating they had common ancestry of origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on TCR sharing patterns.

claim: There were almost no shared TCRs across individuals.
source: There were almost no shared TCRs across individuals, indicating the highly heterogeneous characteristics of T cells among individuals.
evidence: This is based on TCR distribution analysis across individuals.

claim: The starting point of pseudotime was the DN cluster, with CD4+ T cell and CD8+ T cell clusters differentiating toward two different directions.
source: The starting point of pseudotime was the DN cluster, with CD4+ T cell and CD8+ T cell clusters differentiating toward two different directions, suggesting of their distinct developmental paths.
evidence: This is based on pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3j-l.

claim: Two P-tex clusters primarily aggregated at the end of the pseudotime backbone of CD8+ T cells, and presented to be a specific branch originating from T-Tex.
source: Notably, two P-tex clusters primarily aggregated at the end of the pseudotime backbone of CD8+ T cells, and presented to be a specific branch originating from T-Tex, demonstrating its specific activation state and characteristic, which was distinct from other T-Tex cells.
evidence: This is based on pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3j-l.

claim: P-Tex2 was located ahead of P-Tex1 on the pseudotime.
source: Besides, P-Tex2 was located ahead of P-Tex1 on the pseudotime, which was consistent with the results in Figure 2d–e, where P-Tex2 cells mainly entered the S phase of the cell cycle (early phase), while P-Tex1 mainly entered the G2/M phase (later phase).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime trajectory analysis.

claim: Teff cells transformed from an activated to exhausted state (T-Tex cells), and some of the T-Tex cells could further gradually transform into a unique P-Tex subpopulation.
source: Taken together, given that two P-Tex clusters were located at the end of the developmental trajectory of the Teff and T-Tex cells and that P-Tex clusters partially shared TCRs with the T-Tex cluster, we speculated that Teff cells transformed from an activated to exhausted state (T-Tex cells), and some of the T-Tex cells could further gradually transform into a unique P-Tex subpopulation with a highly specific proliferation state.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on trajectory and TCR sharing analysis.

claim: The proliferation rate of P-Tex cells cultured with IL-2 for 15 and 20 days in vitro was much slower than that of T-Tex cells.
source: Unexpectedly, our flow cytometry results showed that the proliferation rate of P-Tex cells cultured with IL-2 for 15 and 20 days in vitro was much slower than that of T-Tex cells (Figure 4a), whereas the cell viability of P-Tex cells was much higher than that of T-Tex cells (Figure 4b–c), indicating that instead of showing high proliferation capacity when stimulated in vitro, the P-Tex cells were mainly characterized by prolonged cell survival.
evidence: This is based on in vitro proliferation experiments shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The cell viability of P-Tex cells was much higher than that of T-Tex cells.
source: Unexpectedly, our flow cytometry results showed that the proliferation rate of P-Tex cells cultured with IL-2 for 15 and 20 days in vitro was much slower than that of T-Tex cells (Figure 4a), whereas the cell viability of P-Tex cells was much higher than that of T-Tex cells (Figure 4b–c), indicating that instead of showing high proliferation capacity when stimulated in vitro, the P-Tex cells were mainly characterized by prolonged cell survival.
evidence: This is based on in vitro cell viability experiments shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: P-Tex cells are mainly characterized by prolonged cell survival rather than high proliferation capacity when stimulated in vitro.
source: Unexpectedly, our flow cytometry results showed that the proliferation rate of P-Tex cells cultured with IL-2 for 15 and 20 days in vitro was much slower than that of T-Tex cells (Figure 4a), whereas the cell viability of P-Tex cells was much higher than that of T-Tex cells (Figure 4b–c), indicating that instead of showing high proliferation capacity when stimulated in vitro, the P-Tex cells were mainly characterized by prolonged cell survival.
evidence: This is an inference based on in vitro experimental results.

claim: P-Tex cells expressed higher levels of proliferation-related marker UBE2C compared to T-Tex cells.
source: Moreover, P-Tex cells expressed higher levels of proliferation-related marker UBE2C, as measured by flow cytometry, and the variations of UBE2C in P-Tex and T-Tex cells between 9 and 16 days were relatively stable (Figure 4d–g).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 4d-g.

claim: Compared with T-Tex cells, P-Tex cells expressed higher exhaustion-related markers (PD1).
source: Besides, compared with T-Tex cells, P-Tex cells expressed higher exhaustion-related markers (PD1), and the expression of PD1 in P-Tex and T-Tex cells gradually increased from day 9 to day 16.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry measurements.

claim: A larger proportion of T-Tex cells produced more cytotoxic-related markers (KLRB1) than P-Tex cells after stimulated with CD3/CD28 microbeads and IL-2 for 9 and 16 days in vitro.
source: Meanwhile, a larger proportion of T-Tex cells produced more cytotoxic-related markers (KLRB1) than P-Tex cells after stimulated with CD3/CD28 microbeads and IL-2 for 9 and 16 days in vitro, whereas the expression of KLRB1 in T-Tex gradually decreased since day 9, and the expression of KLRB1 in P-Tex was relatively stable.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry measurements.

claim: P-Tex cells represent a unique subcluster of the exhausted CD8+ T cells, which was characterized by prolonged cell survival in vitro and could provide modest but persistent anti-tumor effects.
source: Taken together, P-Tex cells represent a unique subcluster of the exhausted CD8+ T cells, which was characterized by prolonged cell survival in vitro and could provide modest but persistent anti-tumor effects.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple in vitro experimental results.

claim: A total of 13,515 cells from tumors (9040 cells) and adjacent normal tissues (4476 cells) were obtained after quality control.
source: After quality control, a total of 13,515 cells from tumors (9040 cells) and adjacent normal tissues (4476 cells) were obtained.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental data.

claim: P-Tex cells highly expressed proliferation- and cell cycle-related genes and functions as the cancer epithelial cluster.
source: We consistently identified that P-Tex cells highly expressed proliferation- and cell cycle-related genes and functions as the cancer epithelial cluster (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq analysis of tumor microenvironment shown in Figure 5b.

claim: P-Tex clusters were predominantly tumor-derived cells.
source: P-Tex clusters were predominantly tumor-derived (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–b) cells.
evidence: This is based on tissue distribution analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a-b.

claim: CDK4 was highly expressed in P-Tex2 cells, cancer epithelial cells, and fibroblasts.
source: Notably, CDK4 was highly expressed in P-Tex2 cells, cancer epithelial cells, and fibroblasts, while MKI67 was highly expressed in P-Tex1 clusters.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: MKI67 was highly expressed in P-Tex1 clusters.
source: Notably, CDK4 was highly expressed in P-Tex2 cells, cancer epithelial cells, and fibroblasts, while MKI67 was highly expressed in P-Tex1 clusters.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: HPV-positive HNSCC patients with higher CDK4 expression levels showed better survival than patients with lower CDK4 expression.
source: And it was interesting that HPV-positive HNSCC patients with higher CDK4 expression levels showed better survival than patients with lower CDK4 expression, whereas HPV-negative HNSCC patients with higher CDK4 expression levels showed worse prognosis (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: HPV-negative HNSCC patients with higher CDK4 expression levels showed worse prognosis.
source: And it was interesting that HPV-positive HNSCC patients with higher CDK4 expression levels showed better survival than patients with lower CDK4 expression, whereas HPV-negative HNSCC patients with higher CDK4 expression levels showed worse prognosis (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Compared with HPV-negative patients, the proportion of P-Tex was higher in the TME of HPV-positive HNSCC patients.
source: Besides, compared with HPV-negative patients, the proportion of P-Tex was higher in the TME of HPV-positive HNSCC patients (TCGA cohort, Figure 5e, Figure 5—figure supplement 2c, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is based on deconvolution analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Abemaciclib inhibited the cell viability of both cancer cells (FD-LSC-1 cells) and P-Tex cells.
source: As expected, abemaciclib inhibited the cell viability of both cancer cells (FD-LSC-1 cells) and P-Tex cells (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is based on in vitro CDK4 inhibition experiments shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The inhibition of CDK4 inhibitor on the cell viability of P-Tex cells might be a potential reason why CDK4 inhibitors were ineffective in treating HPV-positive HNSCC patients.
source: Therefore, we speculated that the inhibition of CDK4 inhibitor on the cell viability of P-Tex cells (which were beneficial to the survival prognosis of HPV-positive HNSCC patients) might be a potential reason why CDK4 inhibitors were ineffective in treating HPV-positive HNSCC patients.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on experimental results and clinical observations.

claim: The interactions between P-Tex and Tex clusters and APCs (especially DCs) in the HNSCC TME were mainly enriched in T cell activation and proliferation signaling pathways, such as CD70-, CD80-, ICOS-, and PD-L1-related signaling pathways.
source: The results showed that the interactions between P-Tex and Tex clusters and APCs (especially DCs) in the HNSCC TME were mainly enriched in T cell activation and proliferation signaling pathways, such as CD70-, CD80-, ICOS-, and PD-L1-related signaling pathways (Figure 6a–b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is based on cell-cell interaction analysis shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: The P-Tex and Tex cells were characterized by the co-localization in the APC aggregation area with significantly higher P-Tex scores and Tex scores than other non-APC areas (p<0.001).
source: The P-Tex and Tex cells were characterized by the co-localization in the APC aggregation area with significantly higher P-Tex scores and Tex scores than other non-APC areas (p<0.001), and the correlations among the three scores in the APC area were higher than those in other non-APC areas.
evidence: This is based on spatial transcriptomics analysis shown in Figure 6d-e.

claim: The activation score of T cells were higher in APC area.
source: As expected, the activation score of T cells were higher in APC area (Figure 6d–e, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is based on spatial transcriptomics analysis shown in Figure 6d-e.

claim: The ligand–receptor interactions of T cell activation and proliferation signaling pathways (CD70-CD27, CD80-ICOS, CD86-CTLA4, CD274-PDCD1) were detected in the APC areas.
source: Besides, the aforementioned ligand–receptor interactions of T cell activation and proliferation signaling pathways (CD70-CD27, CD80-ICOS, CD86-CTLA4, CD274-PDCD1) were also detected in the APC areas (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is based on spatial transcriptomics analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Enriched signaling pathways in APC areas involve the cell cycle, neutrophil activation, and RNA splicing.
source: We also observed enriched signaling pathways in APC areas involving the cell cycle, neutrophil activation, and RNA splicing (Figure 6g), supporting that these antigen-presenting cells play a role in modulating the immune response within the TME by promoting T cell activation (Mehrfeld et al., 2018; Wosen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of spatial transcriptomics data shown in Figure 6g, with citation support.

claim: 90% of the P-Tex cells, bulk Tex, and bulk CD8+ cells enriched within a distance of 25 µm from APCs, forming an intra-tumoral niche.
source: As expected, 90% of the P-Tex cells, bulk Tex, and bulk CD8+ cells enriched within a distance of 25 µm from APCs, forming an intra-tumoral niche (Jansen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on multiplex immunofluorescence distance analysis shown in Figure 7c, with citation support.

claim: P-Tex cells were enriched in the APC aggregation areas, and the signal pathways related to T cell activation and proliferation were activated in these areas.
source: Taken together, P-Tex cells were enriched in the APC aggregation areas, and the signal pathways related to T cell activation and proliferation were activated in these areas, indicating that P-Tex might act as a specific T cell pool that provides modest but persistent effects through its interactions with APCs.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on spatial transcriptomics and multiplex immunofluorescence data.

claim: P-Tex might act as a specific T cell pool that provides modest but persistent effects through its interactions with APCs.
source: Taken together, P-Tex cells were enriched in the APC aggregation areas, and the signal pathways related to T cell activation and proliferation were activated in these areas, indicating that P-Tex might act as a specific T cell pool that provides modest but persistent effects through its interactions with APCs.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: A typical three-stage differentiation trajectory (progenitor–transitional–terminal) has been established to depict the corresponding spatiotemporally sequential alterations of gene signatures, functional characteristics, as well as epigenetic modifications in T cell exhaustion.
source: There is accumulating evidences showing that heterogeneity is a hallmark of T cell exhaustion, and a typical three-stage differentiation trajectory (progenitor–transitional–terminal) has been established to depict the corresponding spatiotemporally sequential alterations of gene signatures, functional characteristics, as well as epigenetic modifications (Beltra et al., 2020; Im and Ha, 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Several previous studies have identified similar proliferation Tex clusters in chronic LCMV-infected mouse models using scRNA-seq.
source: Despite several previous studies have identified similar proliferation Tex clusters in chronic LCMV-infected mouse models using scRNA-seq, little attention was paid to their potential roles in anti-tumor immunity (Miller et al., 2019; Wagle et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about previous literature with citation support.

claim: Little attention was paid to the potential roles of proliferation Tex clusters in anti-tumor immunity.
source: Despite several previous studies have identified similar proliferation Tex clusters in chronic LCMV-infected mouse models using scRNA-seq, little attention was paid to their potential roles in anti-tumor immunity (Miller et al., 2019; Wagle et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: P-Tex was an independent branch of Tex cells and might act as a T cell pool, providing modest but persistent anti-tumor immunity through its prolonged cell survival and highly specialized cytotoxic capacity.
source: In this study, we systematically investigated the functional characteristics and developmental trajectory of P-Tex cells by comparing with other CD8+ T cell clusters. Our results suggested that P-Tex was an independent branch of Tex cells and might act as a T cell pool, providing modest but persistent anti-tumor immunity through its prolonged cell survival and highly specialized cytotoxic capacity.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple experimental results.

claim: The beneficial effect of P-Tex on long-term survival outcomes was only observed in HPV-positive HNSCC who had higher proportion of P-Tex.
source: However, this beneficial on long-term survival outcomes was only observed in HPV-positive HNSCC who had higher proportion of P-Tex.
evidence: This is based on survival analysis and cell proportion analysis in TCGA cohort.

claim: CDK4/6 inhibitors work by specifically inhibiting CDK4/6 proteins, blocking the transition from the G1 to the S phase of the cell cycle and preventing cancer cell progression.
source: CDK4/6 inhibitors (e.g., palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib) are promising drugs for various cancers (Du et al., 2020), working by specifically inhibiting CDK4/6 proteins, blocking the transition from the G1 to the S phase of the cell cycle and preventing cancer cell progression (Álvarez-Fernández and Malumbres, 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of CDK4/6 inhibitors with citation support.

claim: A novel promising P-Tex cluster, which was mainly identified in APC areas of TME, was beneficial to the survival prognosis of HPV-positive HNSCC.
source: Overall, a novel promising P-Tex cluster, which was mainly identified in APC areas of TME, was beneficial to the survival prognosis of HPV-positive HNSCC,.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claim: The inhibitory effect of CDK4 inhibitors on P-Tex cells helps clarify its ineffectiveness in HPV-positive HNSCC patients.
source: Besides, the inhibitory effect of CDK4 inhibitors on P-Tex cells helps clarify its ineffectiveness in HPV-positive HNSCC patients.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on experimental results and clinical observations.
